claims.text: Nanoscale structural inhomogeneities govern the sharp and hysteretic magnetocaloric response of as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloys.
Defect clusters, residual stresses, and compositional inhomogeneities act as pinning centers at phase boundaries between magnetic domains.
The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi alloy has an ordered single-phase hexagonal structure.
The as-deposited alloy undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition.
The first-order transition produces a sharp, large entropy change.
The transition in the as-deposited alloy exhibits pronounced hysteresis.
The untreated as-deposited alloy has limited heat-exchange performance.
A controlled anneal at approximately 300–400 °C is the proposed intervention.
Low-temperature annealing will relieve residual stress and reduce nanoscale defect clusters.
The cited evidence indicates that increasing temperature suppresses stacking faults and nanotwins in CoCrFeMnNi.
Nanoscale defects cause strong phase-boundary pinning during the magnetostructural transition in the as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi alloy.
Annealing-induced defect relaxation will reduce phase-boundary pinning.
Reduced pinning will permit more continuous movement of the phase boundary.
More continuous phase-boundary movement will broaden the magnetostructural transition and distribute the entropy change over a wider temperature interval.
Annealing will reduce hysteretic energy loss per cycle relative to the as-deposited baseline under identical low applied fields.
The predicted effects are bounded to low-field cycles within the magnetostructural-transition temperature window at ambient pressure.
The predicted effects may not extend to high-field conditions or annealing treatments that produce secondary phases.
Failure to observe transition broadening and reduced hysteretic loss after annealing is specified as a falsifying outcome.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as single-phase hexagonal, while the mediator is located at 'phase boundaries between the hexagonal magnetic domains.' Magnetic-domain boundaries can exist within one phase, but calling them phase boundaries conflicts with or at least ambiguously departs from the single-phase description.
